new.title: See the whole city in miniature at the Musée Historique
new.desc: Strasbourg's history museum fills the Grande Boucherie, the city's Renaissance butchers' hall built in 1586 to 1588 beside the Ill. Its star piece is a relief model of Strasbourg from 1727 at 1/600 scale, covering nearly 80 square metres.
new.tip: Find your hotel or your street on the relief model before you look at anything else. The museum is a few steps from the cathedral, ideal for a rainy hour.
new.q: Musée historique de la Ville de Strasbourg, 2 Rue du Vieux-Marché-aux-Poissons

new.title: Admire Église Saint-Paul at the tip of its island
new.desc: The twin spires of Saint-Paul rise 76 metres over the point where the Ill and the Aar meet, at the southern tip of the Île Sainte-Hélène. It was built from 1892 to 1897 as the church of the Protestant German garrison, modelled partly on the Elisabethkirche in Marburg.
new.tip: The church looks best from the riverbanks around it, with the water on both sides. It is a short walk from Place de la République through the Neustadt.

new.title: Spot the crooked tower of Saint-Guillaume
new.desc: This Gothic church in the Krutenau was finished in 1307 and adopted by the boatmen's guild in 1331. Its bell tower of 1667 leans and looks lopsided, and inside lies the double tomb of the brothers Philippe and Ulrich von Werd, landgraves of Alsace.
new.tip: The church is famous for its choir and its Bach Passions, so look out for concerts around Easter. View the tower from the Pont Saint-Guillaume to see the tilt.

new.title: Read with a harbour view at the Médiathèque Malraux
new.desc: The city's main library opened in 2008 inside a former port warehouse on the Presqu'île Malraux, rebuilt in the 1930s for the Seegmuller company. It now spreads over six floors and 11,800 square metres, and the old handling cranes were kept on the quay outside.
new.tip: Entry is free for browsing, and the upper floors look out over the port basins. Walk on along the quays to the Parc de la Citadelle.

new.title: Slip into the galleried courtyard of the Cour du Corbeau
new.desc: An inn stood here from at least 1306, possibly the oldest in Strasbourg, and its guests included Frederick II of Prussia travelling incognito in 1740. Behind the entrance on the quay, a long narrow courtyard is lined with wooden galleries, restored and now part of a hotel.
new.tip: The single entrance is on Place du Corbeau at 1 Quai des Bateliers. Be discreet, as people are staying here, and come back out to the bridge for the view of the quays.

new.title: Wander the garden city of the Stockfeld
new.desc: When Strasbourg demolished slum housing in its old centre from 1907, it rehoused families in a garden city on the southern edge of town inspired by English models. Built from 1910 to 1912, it was cut short by the First World War at 220 homes, and it has been a listed monument since 1996.
new.tip: It is a quiet residential district, so stroll the streets rather than peer into gardens. The Rhine forest of the Neuhof is close by for a longer walk.

new.title: Taste your way through Mireille Oster's gingerbread
new.desc: In a lane of Petite France, Mireille Oster sells handmade pain d'épices in dozens of varieties, from the classic honey and spice loaf to filled and iced versions. Food critics call her the queen of Strasbourg gingerbread, and the shop also sells bredele and candied orange.
new.tip: Ask to taste before you choose; the staff are generous with samples. Gingerbread keeps well, so it is the easiest edible souvenir to carry home.
new.q: Pain d'épices Mireille Oster, 14 Rue des Dentelles, Strasbourg

new.title: Take tea facing the cathedral at Christian
new.desc: Christian is a Strasbourg pastry and chocolate house that has worked for more than forty years. Its tea room on Rue Mercière looks straight up the street at the cathedral facade, and a second shop sits on Rue de l'Outre near Place Kléber.
new.tip: Ask for a table by the window for the cathedral view. Both shops are traditionally closed on Sunday and Monday, so check before you go.

new.title: Order jambon en croûte at the Saint-Sépulcre
new.desc: Known in Alsatian as Hailich Graab, this is one of the oldest and most typical winstubs in Strasbourg, on Rue des Orfèvres. Its reputation was built on ham baked in a bread crust, with munster gratiné and pot-au-feu salad as other house classics.
new.tip: It is open every day, which is handy on Sundays when many winstubs close. Book for dinner, especially in December.
new.q: Au Saint-Sépulcre, 15 Rue des Orfèvres, Strasbourg

new.title: Have a drink on the barge of Café Atlantico
new.desc: Moored on the Quai des Pêcheurs in the Krutenau, Café Atlantico is a bar on a barge, open from breakfast until late. Its deck terrace sits right on the water, facing the old town across the Ill.
new.tip: Locals come for weekend brunch and for evening drinks on the deck; book if you want a terrace table. The Gallia tram stop is a short walk away.
new.q: Café Atlantico, 9A Quai des Pêcheurs, Strasbourg

new.title: Shop like a local at the Boulevard de la Marne market
new.desc: Twice a week a long open-air market sets up along the Boulevard de la Marne near the university, with farmers, cheese and fish stalls among the clothes and household stands. It is one of the city's big neighbourhood markets, far from the tourist centre.
new.tip: It runs on Tuesday and Saturday mornings from 7 to 1; tram C, E or F to Observatoire. Neudorf holds its own market on Place du Marché at the same times.

new.title: Stroll the park of the Château de Pourtalès
new.desc: In the Robertsau, the 18th-century Château de Pourtalès was a society meeting place under Mélanie de Pourtalès, whose guests included Napoleon III, Franz Liszt and Albert Schweitzer. The city bought its 24 hectare park, which is open to the public.
new.tip: The château itself is a private university campus and hotel, so enjoy it from the park. Continue north-east into the Robertsau forest for a longer walk.

new.title: Get lost in the Rhine jungle of the Robertsau forest
new.desc: North of the city along the Rhine, the 493 hectare Robertsau forest is an alluvial woodland so tangled with lianas that parts of it feel like a virgin jungle. Together with the forest of La Wantzenau it became a national nature reserve in 2020, with five ponds and marked trails.
new.tip: Stay on the marked paths, as this is a nature reserve. Bring mosquito repellent in summer, when the backwaters are at their most alive.

new.title: Circle Vauban's moats in the Parc de la Citadelle
new.desc: Vauban built a star-shaped citadel here from 1681 to guard the city towards the Rhine. Two of its bastions, a barbican and some moats survive inside a park laid out in 1964 in the Esplanade quarter, on the edge of the port basins.
new.tip: Families head for the water play area in summer. Combine it with the Médiathèque Malraux, a short walk along the basins.

new.title: Walk the floating pontoon of the Parc du Heyritz
new.desc: Opened in 2014 beside the Hôpital Civil, this 8.7 hectare park wraps around the Bassin de l'Hôpital. A 300 metre pontoon runs across the water past a floating garden, and there is a mirror fountain, a playground and an outdoor gym.
new.tip: On hot days children run through the mirror fountain. Follow the canal path from here to Place de l'Étoile.

new.title: Count the heads on Rosheim's Romanesque church
new.desc: Built around 1150 in pink and yellow sandstone, Saints-Pierre-et-Paul in Rosheim is one of the finest Romanesque churches in Alsace. Inside, one capital is carved with 21 human heads, and the organ was built by André Silbermann in 1733.
new.tip: Walk around the outside before going in: a knight fighting a dragon and other figures perch on the roof and the apse. Rosheim has a station on the line from Strasbourg to Sélestat via Molsheim.

new.title: Admire the butchers' Metzig in Molsheim
new.desc: Molsheim's market square is dominated by the Metzig, the Renaissance hall of the butchers' guild, with a turret dated 1607 and gilded angels added in the 19th century. The town was a Jesuit stronghold, and Ettore Bugatti later built his car factory here.
new.tip: Walk on to the Jesuit church of 1618, with a Silbermann organ. Car fans can visit the Fondation Bugatti in the old Chartreuse museum complex.
new.q: La Metzig, Place de l'Hôtel de Ville, Molsheim

new.title: Face the Romanesque front of Marmoutier abbey
new.desc: Irish monks founded an abbey here around 589, and its church keeps one of the great Romanesque facades of Alsace: a three-arched porch between two square towers, from the 11th century. Inside stands an organ of 1710 by the Silbermanns, restored under Albert Schweitzer in 1955.
new.tip: Marmoutier is a short drive south of Saverne, so pair it with the Château des Rohan. Check the parish noticeboard for organ concerts.

new.title: Step into the Baroque church of Ebersmunster
new.desc: In a small village on the Ill north of Sélestat, the abbey church of Ebersmunster is a burst of south German Baroque. It was rebuilt from 1720 to 1726 after lightning destroyed the previous church, and an André Silbermann organ of 1730 fills the gallery.
new.tip: It is an easy detour from the road between Strasbourg and Sélestat. Look for organ concerts, as the Silbermann instrument is one of the treasures of the church.

new.title: Explore the old and the new in Château de Lichtenberg
new.desc: First mentioned in 1206, this northern Vosges castle was turned into a cannon-proof fortress by Daniel Specklin and burned when Württemberg artillery bombarded it in 1870. A restoration from 1996 by architect Andrea Bruno added bold modern spaces inside the ruined walls.
new.tip: The castle hosts exhibitions and shows, so check the programme. It pairs well with La Petite-Pierre, about 20 minutes away by car.

new.title: Understand Alsace's changing flags at the Mémorial
new.desc: Between 1870 and 1945 Alsatians changed nationality four times, and this museum above Schirmeck tells that story, including the Nazi annexation and the young men forcibly conscripted into the German army, known as the malgré-nous. Opened in 2005, it also covers the building of Europe.
new.tip: The Natzweiler-Struthof memorial is nearby, but doing both in one day is emotionally heavy. Allow at least two hours here.

new.title: Tour the Meteor brewery in Hochfelden
new.desc: Beer has been brewed on this site in Hochfelden since 1640, and Meteor, run by the Haag family since 1898, calls itself the last big independent brewery in Alsace. The family villa opened to visitors in 2016 for 90 minute tours of the brewhouse and cellars, with a tasting.
new.tip: Tours must be booked in advance. From mid-May to mid-September the villa garden turns into an evening biergarten.

new.title: Taste the northernmost wines of Alsace at Cleebourg
new.desc: Far from the main wine route, the vineyards around Cleebourg near Wissembourg were saved by a cooperative founded in 1946. Its members farm around 190 hectares and are known for Auxerrois, alongside Pinot Gris, Riesling and crémant.
new.tip: Ask to try the Auxerrois from the Keimberg hillside. Wissembourg is ten minutes away for lunch.

new.title: Start the wine route with a tasting at Cave du Roi Dagobert
new.desc: The northern end of the Alsace wine route runs through Marlenheim and Traenheim, where this cooperative cellar was founded in 1952 by local growers. It offers tastings of the wines from the hills between Marlenheim and Molsheim.
new.tip: Tastings are free; call ahead to confirm hours, which change with the season. Bring a designated driver or come by bike.

new.title: Eat choucroute at Krautergersheim's cabbage festival
new.desc: The fields around Krautergersheim grow cabbage for sauerkraut, and the village proudly calls itself the choucroute capital. Every autumn since 1974 it has held the Fête de la Choucroute, with choucroute garnie under a big tent, a parade and cabbage-cutting demonstrations.
new.tip: It usually falls on the last weekend of September and the following Saturday. Meal tickets usually go on sale in advance, so check the festival site before you go.

new.title: Stroll the white half-timbered streets of Hunspach
new.desc: Hunspach in northern Alsace is a whole village of whitewashed half-timbered farmhouses with hipped roofs, many from the 18th century. It is one of the most beautiful villages of France and was voted the French favourite village in 2020.
new.tip: Come early or late in the day for empty streets. The Maginot Line fort of Schoenenbourg is just outside the village.

new.title: Go underground in the Maginot fort of Schoenenbourg
new.desc: Completed in the 1930s, this Maginot Line fort hides barracks, kitchens and combat blocks in galleries 18 to 30 metres underground, about 3 kilometres of them. In June 1940 it took more than 3,000 shells and 160 bombs and only surrendered on 1 July, after the armistice.
new.tip: It stays cool underground all year, so bring a jacket even in summer. Opening is seasonal, so check the dates before you go.

new.title: Walk the ramparts of La Petite-Pierre
new.desc: Perched on a sandstone ridge in the northern Vosges, La Petite-Pierre is a fortified old town with a castle first mentioned in 1212 and refortified by Vauban. The castle has housed the Northern Vosges regional nature park since 1977, and its courtyard, garden and craft shop are open to visitors.
new.tip: Follow the rampart path to the old cisterns under the castle. In August the castle hosts the Au Grès du Jazz festival.

new.title: Join the Ami Fritz wedding in Marlenheim
new.desc: Marlenheim marks the northern gateway of the Alsace wine route. Every 15 August the village restages a 19th-century country wedding inspired by L'Ami Fritz, the novel by Erckmann-Chatrian, with costumes, a procession and plenty of local wine.
new.tip: Arrive early to find parking, or come by train. The vineyards of the Marlenberg rise behind the village for a walk afterwards.

new.title: Watch eagles fly over Kintzheim castle
new.desc: Since 1968 the ruined castle of Kintzheim, above Sélestat, has been home to the Volerie des Aigles. Eagles, falcons and vultures, many of them endangered species, fly low over the crowd during the daily demonstrations between the old walls.
new.tip: Opening is seasonal, so check the show times before you go. The Haut-Kœnigsbourg is just up the road for a full day.

new.title: Hike to the Nideck waterfall and the giants' castle
new.desc: Above Oberhaslach, a 25 metre waterfall drops through the forest below the ruins of the Château du Nideck, destroyed by fire in 1636. Legend says giants lived here, and their daughter carried a farmer home as a toy, a tale collected by the Brothers Grimm and retold by Chamisso.
new.tip: The waterfall is an easy walk from the forest car park, and the castle ruins are a short climb further. Go after rain, when the falls are at their best.
